questions_asked: On these Seattle-area highways, is the daily traffic count spread evenly over the day, or does most of it bunch into a few peak-hour rush windows?

On a busy Seattle highway, what mainly makes adding a few self-driving cars help: do they fit into the gaps more smoothly, or do they need a group of cooperating self-driving cars around them before they clearly make a difference?
If I predicted a self-driving lane would cut peak-hour delays, what delay improvement would count as a real win worth building it?
expert_answers: Most of it bunches into peak windows. On these Seattle-area routes (I-5, I-90, I-405, SR-520), the daily count is strongly peaked: the AM and PM commute periods (roughly 6–9 a.m. and 3–7 p.m.) carry a disproportionate share, with the peak hour typically around 8–10% of the daily total and the two peak windows together often 25–35%. Off-peak and overnight hours carry the remainder at much lower rates. So the daily average is not a good proxy for the capacity-critical flow; the peak-hour volume is what drives congestion.

Mainly the latter: a few isolated self-driving cars mixed into human-driven traffic produce little capacity gain. The clear benefit comes when self-driving cars can cooperate with each other — platooning, short coordinated headways, smoother merging — which requires a meaningful cluster of them, not just a scattered few. So the effect is strongly nonlinear in the self-driving share: negligible at low percentages, and pronounced only once enough cooperating vehicles are present to form platoons and interact with each other. A lone self-driving car surrounded by human drivers mostly behaves conservatively and gains little.

A real win would be a substantial cut in peak-hour delay, not a marginal one. As an empirical judgment: a dedicated self-driving lane is worth building if it reduces peak-hour delay for the affected traffic by roughly 20–30% or more, and/or raises peak-hour throughput enough to move the bottleneck back to free-flow for most of the peak. Below about 10% improvement, the gain is within normal day-to-day variation and wouldn't justify the lost general-purpose lane capacity. The threshold should be judged on the peak window, not the daily average, since that's where the delay concentrates.
